connector: You just finished The Whipping Boy, a made-up story about a prince in a castle. This week you read true articles about real castles. Who lived there, and what did they do all day? Look for the one big idea the article keeps coming back to.

a.raw: king john stayed at windsor castle
a.why: King is a title right before his name, so it gets a capital K. John is a name. Windsor Castle is the name of one place, so both words get capitals. A period ends the sentence.

b.why: Queen is a title right before her name, so it gets a capital Q. Eleanor is a name, and England is the name of a place. A period ends the sentence.

fill1.h1: It means carry. You can find it in import and export.
fill1.why: trans + port = transport: to carry across.

fill2.h1: It means shape. A butterfly changes this.
fill2.why: trans + form = transform: to change into a new shape.

fill3.h1: Look at the word list above. It is the last word in the list.
fill3.why: trans + late = translate: to carry words across into another language.

fill4.h1: It is a six-letter word. Your mom or dad is one.
fill4.why: trans + parent = transparent: you can see across, or through, it.

vcloze1.h1: This place was built to keep enemies out. Look at the word with fort in it.
vcloze1.why: A fortress is a strong building built to keep enemies out.

vcloze2.h1: Find the word for the strongest tower inside the castle.
vcloze2.why: The keep is the strongest inner tower.

vcloze3.h1: These people cooked, cleaned and cared for the family.
vcloze3.why: Servants worked in someone else’s home.

vcloze4.h1: Find the word for a boy training to be a knight.
vcloze4.why: A page trained in a noble’s home to become a knight.

match.fortress: A fortress is a building. Look for the meaning about a strong building.
match.keep: The keep is one part of a castle. Look for the meaning about a tower.
match.servant: A servant is a person. Look for the meaning about working in someone’s home.
match.page: A page is a boy. Look for the meaning about training to be a knight.

wordgame.title: Illuminate the Page
wordgame.sub: Every right answer paints part of a medieval book page.
wordgame.todo: Read the question. Tap the answer you think is right. A right answer paints the next part of the page.
wordgame.win: Today’s 8 parts are painted. Come back next lesson to keep painting.
wordgame.winWeek: Your page is finished, from the gold letter to the last line!
wordgame.look: This week’s game is a page from a medieval book, before it is painted. Long ago, books were written and painted by hand. A painted page is called illuminated, because the gold makes it shine. Each right answer paints one part. Day 1 paints the big gold capital letter. Day 2 paints the border, Day 3 the little picture, and Day 4 the lines of writing.

items.why: trans + mit: to send across. Trance starts with t r a n, but nothing goes across.

glossary.m: the most important point an author makes. The whole article keeps coming back to it.
one fact from the article that helps prove the central idea
a time in history about 500 to 1,500 years ago, when there were castles, knights and kings in Europe
vowel, consonant, consonant, vowel. A word with this pattern splits between the two consonants, like nap · kin.
one beat in a word. Basket has two: bas · ket.
stretching the truth on purpose, so much that nobody believes it, like “I’m so hungry I could eat a horse.”
writing that explains or teaches facts about a topic
the question you want your notes to answer
working hard and carefully, and not giving up

cards.title: Job Spotlight: The Page
cards.sub: A real job in the Middle Ages
cards.todo: Read about this real job. Then read the two questions and the article.
text: A page was a boy from a noble family. At about seven years old, he went to live in a lord’s castle.
He served at meals, carried messages, and learned to ride and to use a sword.
At about fourteen, a page could become a squire, the next step toward being a knight.

transcripts.welcome: Hi, it’s Opti. You just finished The Whipping Boy. This week you read true articles about real life long ago. Today: a castle. Who lived there, and what did they do all day?
transcripts.guide1: Word work first. You’ll meet a word part that means across, sort names that get capital letters, and split words between two consonants.
transcripts.guide2: Read the castle article. Look for the one big idea it keeps coming back to.
transcripts.guide3: Today you pick your own topic about medieval life, one you will explain.

notes.wordParts: The word part trans means across. transport = to carry across. translate = to carry words across into another language. Some words only start with t r a n, like tranquil (calm).
notes.grammar: Capital letters start every sentence and every important word in a name: people (Queen Eleanor), places (Tower of London) and titles. Small words like the, of and in stay small inside a name or title, unless they come first.
notes.spelling: VCCV means vowel, consonant, consonant, vowel. Split the word between the two consonants: bas · ket, tun · nel. Letters like ph and th stay together.
notes.wgrd: The central idea is the most important point an author makes. A detail is one fact that helps prove it.
vocab: a large, strong building built to resist attack
the strongest, innermost tower of a castle
a person who works in someone else’s household
a young boy in training at a noble household, learning to become a knight

mods.script: [curious] Have you ever walked across a bridge? You start on one side and end up on the other. There's a word part that means across. Trans. T, r, a, n, s. Trans, plus Pacific, makes transpacific: across the Pacific Ocean. But careful! Tranquil starts with t, r, a, n, and it just means calm. Nothing goes across. mods.script: [warmly] Some words are names, and names get capital letters. Listen. Stories say Robin Hood lived in Sherwood Forest. Robin Hood names a person. Sherwood Forest names a place. Every important word in a name gets a capital. A book title does too, like The Wind in the Willows. But little words inside, like in and the, stay small. Tap Now check your thinking. So I split right between the two consonants. Pup. Pet. Say the words in Group A and Group B out loud, and tap See the Rule. Then sort all eight words.

Box one, change the opener: In the hot kitchen, the cook stirred the soup. Box two, a stronger verb: The cook swirled the soup. Box three, add a detail: The tired cook stirred the thick soup. Now it's your turn, one box at a time. If you get stuck, tap Show one way.

virtue.name: diligence
virtue.title: Diligence Watch: Is someone working hard?

items.t: Servants cooked food, cleaned, and cared for the horses.
items.why: They did hard jobs every day to keep the castle going.

items.t: The keep was the strongest part of the castle.
items.why: That is a fact about a building, not about someone working.

items.t: Young boys from noble families trained for years as pages.
items.why: Training for years takes steady, hard work.
